In a classic Bloody Mary.Vodka: The spirit base of the drink. It was first mixed with tomato juice in the 1920s or 30s at Harry's New York Bar in Paris, by tradition.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Tomato juice: The drink's body. Tomato juice was a popular American beverage by the 1930s, partly promoted at health spas.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Worcestershire sauce: A fermented sauce of anchovies, tamarind and vinegar from Worcester, England, which gives the cocktail its savory depth.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Tabasco: Made from aged peppers, vinegar and salt on Avery Island, Louisiana, by the McIlhenny family since 1868.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Celery salt: Often used to rim the glass, it adds an earthy savor. Celery salt is traditionally a mix of ground celery seed and salt.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Lemon juice: Citrus adds the sharp brightness that cuts through the tomato's heaviness. Some bartenders add a wedge on the rim as well.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Black pepper: Freshly cracked pepper adds heat. Black pepper was once so valuable in Europe that it was called 'black gold'.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Horseradish: Its sinus-clearing kick comes from compounds released when the root is grated. They fade fast, which is why prepared horseradish is bottled in vinegar.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Celery stick: The garnish that doubles as a stirrer. It is said to have started by accident at a Chicago hotel bar in the 1960s, when a guest stirred with a stalk.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Rum: Rum goes into a Dark 'n' Stormy or a daiquiri, not a Bloody Mary. Swap vodka for rum and you have changed the cocktail entirely.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Tequila: Replace vodka with tequila and you get a Bloody Maria. It is a classic variation, but not the classic version.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Orange juice: Orange juice belongs in a screwdriver or mimosa. Sweet citrus clashes with the Bloody Mary's savory spice profile.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Cranberry juice: This ruby juice powers the Cape Codder and Cosmopolitan, which are vodka drinks too, but not the tomato-based Bloody Mary.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Mint leaves: Mint is for mojitos and juleps. Its cooling freshness would fight the peppery, savory profile of a Bloody Mary.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Simple syrup: Equal parts sugar and water is a bartender's staple for sours and old fashioneds, but a Bloody Mary is savory and wants no sweetener.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Cream: Cream turns up in a White Russian or Brandy Alexander. Adding it to tomato juice would curdle and ruin the drink.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Coffee liqueur: Kahlúa-style liqueur defines the White Russian and espresso martini, whose sweetness has no place in a savory tomato cocktail.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Coconut cream: This is the soul of a piña colada. Coconut's rich tropical sweetness would clash with the tomato and spice of a Bloody Mary.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Grenadine: A pomegranate syrup that gives the Tequila Sunrise its red gradient. Real grenadine is pomegranate, though many bottles are not.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Triple sec: This orange liqueur is key to margaritas and cosmopolitans. It is a sweet citrus note that the Bloody Mary lacks.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Ginger beer: The spicy fizz that makes a Moscow Mule and Dark 'n' Stormy. It is an unusual swap with tomato, so it is absent here.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Egg white: Egg white gives whiskey sours and pisco sours their silky foam. A classic Bloody Mary has none.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Cola: Cola mixes with rum or whiskey, not tomato juice. A Bloody Mary stays savory and sour, with no caramel sweetness.
In a classic Bloody Mary.Prosecco: Prosecco bubbles in Aperol spritzes and Bellinis. Mixed with tomato juice it would go flat and strange.

Peaks over 8000 metres.Everest: At 8,849 m, the highest mountain above sea level. The Nepalese call it Sagarmatha, and the Tibetans Chomolungma.
Peaks over 8000 metres.K2: The world's second-highest, at 8,611 m, in the Karakoram. It is nicknamed the Savage Mountain, since climbing it is so dangerous.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Kangchenjunga: The world's third-highest at 8,586 m, on the Nepal-India border. Until 1852 it was thought to be the tallest.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Lhotse: The fourth-highest at 8,516 m, joined to Everest by the South Col. Its name is Tibetan for 'south peak'.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Makalu: The fifth-highest at 8,485 m, in the Himalaya. Its shape is a nearly perfect four-sided pyramid.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Cho Oyu: At 8,188 m, one of the less technical eight-thousanders. Its Tibetan name means 'Turquoise Goddess'.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Dhaulagiri: A peak of 8,167 m in Nepal, whose name means 'white mountain' in Sanskrit. It was the highest known mountain until 1808.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Manaslu: At 8,163 m, the eighth-highest mountain. Its name comes from Sanskrit for 'mountain of the spirit', and Japanese climbers first reached its summit.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Nanga Parbat: A peak of 8,126 m in Pakistan, nicknamed the 'Killer Mountain', for the many climbers who died on its early attempts.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Annapurna: In 1950, this became the first 8,000 m peak ever climbed, by a French expedition. It is among the deadliest, at 8,091 m.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Kilimanjaro: A trap: Africa's highest, at 5,895 m. A dormant volcano that stands alone, it is far shy of 8,000 m.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Mont Blanc: A trap: the highest peak in the Alps at about 4,800 m, only about half the height needed here.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Matterhorn: A trap: the pyramid on the Swiss-Italian border is iconic, but at 4,478 m it is far from 8,000.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Denali: North America's highest at about 6,190 m, in Alaska. It was formerly called Mount McKinley.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Aconcagua: A trap: it is the highest mountain outside Asia, at about 6,960 m, but still short of 8,000 m.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Elbrus: A trap: Europe's highest mountain, at 5,642 m, in the Caucasus. A dormant volcano, but far below 8,000 m.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Mount Fuji: A trap: Japan's sacred volcano rises 3,776 m, famous but less than half the height needed.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Mauna Kea: Measured from its base on the ocean floor, it's taller than Everest, but only 4,207 m above sea level.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Ama Dablam: A famous Himalayan peak, at 6,812 m. Its name means 'mother's necklace', but it's too small.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Ben Nevis: A trap: Britain's highest, at 1,345 m. It is a fine walk, but hardly an eight-thousander.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Vinson: A trap: Antarctica's highest peak, at 4,892 m. It is remote and cold, but nowhere near 8,000 m.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Mount Kenya: A trap: Africa's second-highest, at about 5,199 m, an extinct volcano on the equator. Far below 8,000 m.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Chimborazo: At 6,263 m the farthest point from Earth's centre, because the Earth bulges at the equator. Not above 8,000, though.
Peaks over 8000 metres.Mount Cook: A trap: New Zealand's highest peak, at 3,724 m, also known by the Maori name Aoraki. Well below 8,000 m.

Real demonyms (what locals are called).Neapolitan: A person from Naples, also a style of pizza and a three-flavour ice cream.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Haligonian: Residents of Halifax, Nova Scotia, take the name from Haligonia, the Latinised form of the city's name.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Dubliner: A person from Dublin, and also the title of James Joyce's short story collection.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Parisian: Someone from Paris, also describing the city's famous style and the accent of its speech.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Venetian: From Venice. Venetian blinds probably take their name from the city, though their exact origin is unclear.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Florentine: From Florence, and also a cooking term for dishes with spinach.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Sydneysider: A proud resident of Sydney, a word used across Australia.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Monegasque: A citizen of Monaco, the tiny principality, where fewer than a quarter of residents actually hold citizenship.

Real demonyms (what locals are called).Manchesterian: Not a real word, because people from Manchester are Mancunians.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Madridian: Not the real term, since people from Madrid are called madrileños in Spanish.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Moscowite: A common misspelling, the correct form is Muscovite.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Glasgowite: Not real, the proper term for a Glasgow native is Glaswegian.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Liverpoolian: Not used, because the proper term is Liverpudlian, or Scouser informally.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Dublinese: Not a real demonym, since people from Dublin are Dubliners.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Parisite: Not a real word, since Parisian is correct, and parasite is another thing entirely.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Venician: A misspelling of Venetian, which has the T.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Napleser: Not a real word, since people from Naples are Neapolitans.
Real demonyms (what locals are called).Tokyan: Not the usual word, since people from Tokyo are called Tokyoites.

Greek letters (used all over science).Alpha: The first letter, which gave us the phrase alpha and omega; in science it names alpha particles and alpha waves in the brain.
Greek letters (used all over science).Beta: The second letter, used for beta particles and beta decay; software testers borrowed it for pre-release versions.
Greek letters (used all over science).Gamma: The third letter, naming gamma rays, the most energetic light; Paul Villard discovered them in 1900.
Greek letters (used all over science).Delta: The fourth letter, shaped like a triangle; scientists use it for change, and river mouths are named for its shape.
Greek letters (used all over science).Epsilon: The fifth letter, whose name means simple e; mathematicians use it for a vanishingly tiny quantity.
Greek letters (used all over science).Theta: The eighth letter, usually the symbol for an angle in geometry, and for slow brain waves in sleep.
Greek letters (used all over science).Lambda: Used in physics for wavelength; Greek soldiers painted it on shields, and it appears in the Half-Life game logo.
Greek letters (used all over science).Sigma: Capital sigma means sum in math, and lowercase sigma stands for standard deviation in statistics.
Greek letters (used all over science).Omega: The last letter, meaning great O; physicists use it for electrical resistance in ohms and for angular velocity.
Greek letters (used all over science).Pi: The sixteenth letter, now famous as 3.14159..., the circle ratio, whose digits never end or repeat.
Greek letters (used all over science).Rho: Stands for density in physics; its capital looks like a Latin P, which confuses newcomers.
Greek letters (used all over science).Phi: Stands for the golden ratio, about 1.618, which shows up in some spirals, and is also used in physics for angles and magnetic flux.
Greek letters (used all over science).Psi: The wave function in quantum mechanics is written with it, and the letter is also the root of psychology, from the Greek for soul.
Greek letters (used all over science).Mu: Stands for micro, a millionth, and for the coefficient of friction in physics.
Greek letters (used all over science).Aleph: A trap: the first Hebrew letter, and Georg Cantor used it to name different sizes of infinity.
Greek letters (used all over science).Gimel: A trap: the third Hebrew letter, whose name means camel, and it's also used in numerical value for three.
Greek letters (used all over science).Thorn: A trap: an Old English and Old Norse letter that made the th sound; the ye in Ye Olde was really a thorn.
Greek letters (used all over science).Bravo: A trap: this belongs to the NATO phonetic alphabet, used to spell letters clearly over radio, not to Greek.
Greek letters (used all over science).Tango: A trap: the NATO alphabet's word for T, chosen because it sounds clear in noisy radio.
Greek letters (used all over science).Kilo: A trap: the NATO word for K; it also happens to be a metric prefix meaning thousand, but it is not a Greek letter.
Greek letters (used all over science).Zulu: A trap: the NATO word for Z, and also the time zone label for UTC in aviation and military.
Greek letters (used all over science).Echo: A trap: in the NATO alphabet E is Echo; in Greek myth Echo was a nymph, not a letter.
Greek letters (used all over science).Sierra: A trap: the NATO word for S, borrowed from Spanish for mountain range.
Greek letters (used all over science).Oscar: A trap: the NATO word for O, and not to be confused with Omicron, the Greek letter for short o.

Units of mass.Gram: A thousandth of a kilogram, defined originally as the mass of a cubic centimeter of water; a paperclip weighs about one gram.
Units of mass.Kilogram: The last SI unit tied to a physical object, a platinum cylinder in Paris, until 2019 when a constant of physics replaced it.
Units of mass.Pound: The abbreviation lb comes from the Latin libra, and one pound is exactly 0.45359237 kilograms.
Units of mass.Ounce: There are 16 in a pound, and there is a separate troy ounce, used for gold, that is a bit heavier.
Units of mass.Ton: The US short ton is 2,000 pounds, and the British long ton is 2,240, which is why people say metric tonne for clarity.
Units of mass.Stone: A British unit equal to 14 pounds, still used for body weight in the UK and Ireland.
Units of mass.Carat: Equal to 200 milligrams, used for gemstones, and it comes from the carob seed that traders once used as a counterweight.
Units of mass.Tonne: A metric ton of 1,000 kilograms, about the weight of a small car.
Units of mass.Milligram: A thousandth of a gram; a single grain of table salt weighs roughly half a milligram or so.
Units of mass.Grain: A tiny unit of about 65 milligrams, originally based on a grain of barley, and still used for bullets and medicines.
Units of mass.Karat: A trap: spelled almost like carat, but it measures gold purity, with 24 karat being pure gold, not mass.
Units of mass.Liter: A trap: a measure of volume. One liter of water happens to weigh a kilogram, but it's still volume.
Units of mass.Gallon: A trap: volume, as in gasoline, with a US gallon at about 3.8 liters.
Units of mass.Pint: A trap: a liquid volume, and the old rhyme says a pint's a pound the world around, which is only roughly right for water.
Units of mass.Fluid ounce: A trap: the word ounce confuses people, but a fluid ounce measures volume, not weight.
Units of mass.Meter: A trap: a unit of length; one meter is slightly longer than a yard.
Units of mass.Acre: A trap: a measure of land area, and a football field with end zones is about 1.3 acres.
Units of mass.Joule: A trap: it measures energy, and lifting a small apple one meter takes about one joule.
Units of mass.Calorie: A trap: a unit of energy, not of mass; a food Calorie is actually 1,000 small calories.
Units of mass.Knot: A trap: speed at sea, not mass, with one knot at about 1.85 km per hour.
Units of mass.Fathom: A trap: a length of six feet, used for sea depth.
Units of mass.Hectare: A trap: a land area of 10,000 square meters, not mass.
Units of mass.Watt: A trap: a unit of power, joules per second, named for James Watt of steam engine fame.
Units of mass.Bushel: A trap: it measures volume of dry goods, like grain, though in practice farmers also convert it to weight.

Things the human body produces.Saliva: You make roughly a litre a day, and it contains an enzyme that starts digesting starch before food reaches the stomach.
Things the human body produces.Tears: There are three kinds, basal, reflex and emotional, and emotional ones contain extra proteins and hormones.
Things the human body produces.Sweat: It is nearly odourless on its own; the smell comes from skin bacteria feasting on it.
Things the human body produces.Earwax: Its type, wet or dry, is set by a single gene, and it is more often dry among East Asians.
Things the human body produces.Mucus: You make a litre or so daily, mostly swallowed, and it traps dust and germs on their way in.
Things the human body produces.Bile: Made by the liver and stored in the gallbladder to break up fats, and it also gives stool its brown colour.
Things the human body produces.Insulin: A pancreas hormone first purified in 1921 by Banting and Best, which turned diabetes into a manageable condition.
Things the human body produces.Red blood cells: Your bone marrow turns out about two million every second.
Things the human body produces.Stomach acid: It is hydrochloric acid with a pH of about 1 to 2, and the stomach's lining renews itself so it does not digest itself.
Things the human body produces.Melatonin: The brain's pineal gland releases it in darkness, nudging you toward sleep.
Things the human body produces.Keratin: The same tough protein as in hair and nails, and also in horn, feathers and claws.
Things the human body produces.Vitamin D: Your skin makes it with sunlight, which is why it is called the sunshine vitamin.
Things the human body produces.Cholesterol: The liver makes most of it, and cells need it for their membranes and for hormones.
Things the human body produces.Vitamin C: A trap: most mammals make their own, but humans, other primates and guinea pigs lost the ability, so we must eat it.
Things the human body produces.Iron: An element, so no living thing can make it; your body recycles it and loses only a trace each day.
Things the human body produces.Calcium: An element, so it cannot be made; about 99% of the body's store sits in bones and teeth.
Things the human body produces.Fiber: Plant carbohydrate we cannot digest, though gut bacteria ferment some of it.
Things the human body produces.Caffeine: Plants like coffee and tea make it, as a natural pesticide.
Things the human body produces.Chlorophyll: The green pigment in plants; people do not make it, which is why humans cannot photosynthesise.
Things the human body produces.Penicillin: Made by Penicillium mould, not by humans.
Things the human body produces.Sodium: An element the body needs but cannot make; sweat is salty because it carries some.
Things the human body produces.Iodine: We need it for thyroid hormones, and iodised salt was introduced in the 1920s to prevent goitre.
Things the human body produces.Zinc: A trace metal we must eat; oysters are among the richest sources.
Things the human body produces.Silk: Made by silkworms, and a single cocoon is one thread up to around a kilometre long.

Famous movie dogs.Lassie: Lassie was always played by male collies, all descendants of the first Pal, since males keep fuller coats and look bigger on screen.
Famous movie dogs.Beethoven: The 1992 comedy's slobbering St. Bernard drooled his way through a string of sequels; real St. Bernards can top 150 pounds.
Famous movie dogs.Toto: Toto was a Cairn terrier named Terry, who reportedly earned more per week on The Wizard of Oz than many of the human actors.
Famous movie dogs.Hooch: Hooch is a drooling Dogue de Bordeaux who wrecks Tom Hanks's tidy life as his unlikely police partner in Turner & Hooch (1989).
Famous movie dogs.Marley: Marley & Me was based on columnist John Grogan's true story of his unruly Labrador, and many different dogs played the role.
Famous movie dogs.Bolt: Disney's Bolt is a white Swiss shepherd who believes his TV superpowers are real, until a trip across America proves otherwise.
Famous movie dogs.Lady: Lady and the Tramp (1955) was Disney's first animated feature in widescreen CinemaScope, with a cocker spaniel as its heroine.
Famous movie dogs.Tramp: A streetwise mutt who shows pampered Lady the world beyond her fence, and shares the most famous spaghetti dinner in film history.
Famous movie dogs.Pongo: Dalmatians are born pure white, and their spots only appear after a couple of weeks, so Pongo's 15 puppies began as blank slates.
Famous movie dogs.Old Yeller: The 1957 Disney film of Fred Gipson's novel left generations of kids in tears, and its title became shorthand for a sad ending.
Famous movie dogs.Benji: The scruffy star of the 1974 film was a shelter mutt named Higgins, who became a long-running screen hero after his adoption.
Famous movie dogs.Dug: In Up, a collar translates Dug's thoughts into speech, which is why his attention keeps getting hijacked by squirrels mid-sentence.
Famous movie dogs.Gromit: Wallace's dog has no mouth at all; Aardman's animators give him a rich personality with just his brow and a few tiny movements.
Famous movie dogs.Garfield: A trap: Garfield is a cat. The lasagna-loving orange tabby hates Mondays, and the dog in his strip is the drooling Odie.
Famous movie dogs.Sylvester: A cat, not a dog; his name echoes Felis silvestris, the European wildcat, and he spends his career failing to catch Tweety.
Famous movie dogs.Tom: A cat, not a dog; Tom and Jerry won seven Academy Awards for animated shorts, more than almost any other cartoon series.
Famous movie dogs.Puss in Boots: A cat, not a dog; this booted trickster comes from a fairy tale published by Charles Perrault in 1697, long before Shrek.
Famous movie dogs.Babe: A pig, not a dog; the 1995 film about a piglet who herds sheep won an Oscar for visual effects and was nominated for Best Picture.
Famous movie dogs.Bambi: A deer, not a dog; Bambi began in Felix Salten's 1923 Austrian novel, which is a much darker story than Disney's film.
Famous movie dogs.Dumbo: An elephant, not a dog; the 1941 film runs only about an hour, making it one of Disney's shortest animated features.
Famous movie dogs.Simba: A lion, not a dog; Simba is simply the Swahili word for lion, and Disney's story borrows plot ideas from Hamlet.
Famous movie dogs.Stuart Little: A mouse, not a dog; E. B. White's 1945 book about a mouse born to a human family came out before his famous Charlotte's Web.
Famous movie dogs.Remy: A rat, not a dog; Remy cooks in Paris in Ratatouille, and the Pixar team researched the film by studying real restaurant kitchens.
Famous movie dogs.Mr. Bigglesworth: Dr. Evil's hairless Sphynx cat is a cat, not a dog, and he is stroked in the villain's lair in a nod to Bond's Blofeld.

Ghosts in film and TV.Casper: Casper the Friendly Ghost began in a 1930s story and appeared in 1940s cartoons, as a ghost who wants friends.
Ghosts in film and TV.Slimer: Slimer from Ghostbusters was nicknamed 'Onionhead' by the crew, inspired partly by John Belushi's gluttony.
Ghosts in film and TV.Nearly Headless Nick: Nick was beheaded in an incomplete fashion, and leads Gryffindor's ghosts and a death-day party.
Ghosts in film and TV.Moaning Myrtle: Myrtle haunts a Hogwarts girls' bathroom, and she died when she looked into the Basilisk's eyes.
Ghosts in film and TV.Beetlejuice: Beetlejuice, a 'bio-exorcist', has a name that sounds like the star Betelgeuse, and he is summoned by saying it three times.
Ghosts in film and TV.Jacob Marley: In A Christmas Carol (1843), Marley's ghost drags chains forged from his own greed.
Ghosts in film and TV.Bloody Baron: The Bloody Baron, Slytherin's ghost, is covered in silver blood, and he killed the Grey Lady.
Ghosts in film and TV.Fat Friar: The Fat Friar is Hufflepuff's jolly ghost, who always welcomed newcomers with kindness.
Ghosts in film and TV.Grey Lady: The Grey Lady is Ravenclaw's ghost, Helena, the daughter of founder Rowena Ravenclaw.
Ghosts in film and TV.Dracula: Dracula is a vampire, which is undead and physical rather than a ghost, from Bram Stoker's 1897 novel.
Ghosts in film and TV.Frankenstein: Frankenstein's creature is assembled from body parts and brought to life, so he's a physical being, not a spirit.
Ghosts in film and TV.The Mummy: Mummies are preserved corpses rather than spirits, and Boris Karloff's 1932 film popularized the monster.
Ghosts in film and TV.The Wolf Man: The Wolf Man is a living man cursed by a bite, as in Lon Chaney Jr.'s 1941 film.
Ghosts in film and TV.Edward Cullen: Edward is a vampire in Twilight, a physical creature, with skin that sparkles in sunlight.
Ghosts in film and TV.Mavis: Mavis is a young vampire in Hotel Transylvania, physical and alive in her own way, not a ghost.
Ghosts in film and TV.Herman Munster: Herman is a Frankenstein-like monster on The Munsters, flesh and bone, not a spirit.
Ghosts in film and TV.Gollum: Gollum is a corrupted hobbit-like creature, played by Andy Serkis, and he's very much alive.
Ghosts in film and TV.Dobby: Dobby is a house-elf who died but never haunts Hogwarts, buried by Harry at Shell Cottage.
Ghosts in film and TV.Vecna: Vecna is a once-human villain who uses the Upside Down, but he's a living being, not a ghost.
Ghosts in film and TV.Voldemort: Voldemort spent years as a disembodied spirit, but he regained his body in Goblet of Fire, so he's no ghost.
Ghosts in film and TV.Dementor: Dementors are soul-eating wraith-like creatures, not ghosts, and only a Patronus repels them.
Ghosts in film and TV.Count Olaf: Count Olaf is a living, greedy villain who schemes for the Baudelaire fortune, not a spirit.
Ghosts in film and TV.Morticia: Morticia is a living, if macabre, matriarch of the Addams Family, not a ghost.
Ghosts in film and TV.Medusa: Medusa is a Gorgon from Greek myth, a monster with snakes for hair, not a ghost.

Real Oscar categories.Best Picture: The night's final award. Wings, a 1927 silent film about fighter pilots, won the first one, and the Oscars have honored a best picture ever since.
Real Oscar categories.Best Director: Kathryn Bigelow became the first woman to win this award, for The Hurt Locker, at the 2010 ceremony.
Real Oscar categories.Best Actor: Daniel Day-Lewis is the only three-time winner here, for My Left Foot, There Will Be Blood and Lincoln.
Real Oscar categories.Best Actress: Katharine Hepburn holds the record with four wins in this category, across a career spanning more than 50 years.
Real Oscar categories.Best Original Score: This rewards a composer's original music for the film. John Williams has been nominated for it dozens of times, more than any living person in any category.
Real Oscar categories.Best Visual Effects: Awarded for the illusions that audiences should never spot. Early winners of this prize included Star Wars-era pioneers, and today the credits run to hundreds of artists.
Real Oscar categories.Best Film Editing: Editors say their best work is invisible. Winners here often also take Best Picture, since a film's rhythm is built in this stage.
Real Oscar categories.Best Costume Design: Edith Head won eight Oscars in this category, more than any other woman has won in any category.
Real Oscar categories.Best Cinematography: Roger Deakins went through 13 nominations before finally winning, for Blade Runner 2049, then won again for 1917.
Real Oscar categories.Best Original Song: This honors a new song with lyrics written for the film, such as Let It Go or Skyfall, rather than the film's instrumental music.
Real Oscar categories.Best Sound: This award covers the whole soundscape of dialogue, effects and music mixing, so loud war and music films tend to dominate it.
Real Oscar categories.Best Villain: Villains are celebrated at the MTV Movie Awards, not the Oscars. The Academy gives acting prizes by role size, not by good versus evil.
Real Oscar categories.Best Comedy: The Oscars have no comedy category, so funny films compete against dramas. The Golden Globes split the two, which is why comedies rarely win Best Picture.
Real Oscar categories.Best Kiss: The MTV Movie Awards created a Best Kiss trophy, and it has gone to everything from romantic leads to rival pairs. The Academy never has.
Real Oscar categories.Best Fight: Fight scenes are honored by MTV, not the Academy. Stunt performers long went without an Oscar, a gap the Academy has recently moved to close.
Real Oscar categories.Best Trailer: Trailers have their own Golden Trailer Awards. The Academy has never judged a film's advertising, only the film itself.
Real Oscar categories.Best Sequel: A sequel competes in the regular categories. The Godfather Part II won Best Picture in 1975, making it the first sequel to do so.
Real Oscar categories.Best Ensemble: The Academy has no ensemble prize. The closest honor is the SAG Awards' cast prize, though a Best Casting category is being added from 2026.
Real Oscar categories.Best Hero: Heroes get fan-voted prizes at MTV's show; the Oscars honor performances, not character types.
Real Oscar categories.Best Musical: The Oscars give no separate prize for musicals. Chicago won Best Picture against dramas in 2003, and the Golden Globes alone split genres.
Real Oscar categories.Best Soundtrack: The Grammys honor soundtrack albums. The Oscars split the music into Original Score and Original Song instead.
Real Oscar categories.Best Cameo: A cameo has no award, though a brief role can win Best Supporting Actor. Beatrice Straight won for about five minutes of screen time in Network.
Real Oscar categories.Best Twist: Surprise endings aren't a category, though they often win screenplay prizes. The Sixth Sense twist earned nominations but not the trophy.
Real Oscar categories.Best Remake: Remakes compete in the regular categories. The Departed, a remake of Hong Kong's Infernal Affairs, won Best Picture in 2007.

Operas by Puccini.La Bohème: The 1896 opera follows poor artists in Paris and Mimì's fatal illness. Its premiere was conducted by the young Arturo Toscanini.
Operas by Puccini.Tosca: Set in Rome in 1800, it ends with the heroine leaping from the Castel Sant'Angelo. Its aria Vissi d'arte is a soprano staple.
Operas by Puccini.Madama Butterfly: Cio-Cio-San's tragedy flopped at La Scala in 1904, then Puccini revised it. Its Humming Chorus is among opera's most tender moments.
Operas by Puccini.Turandot: Puccini died in 1924 before finishing it, and Franco Alfano completed the ending. Nessun dorma comes from this opera.
Operas by Puccini.Gianni Schicchi: Puccini's only comic opera, a one-act farce about a forged will. O mio babbino caro, often heard alone, comes from here.
Operas by Puccini.Manon Lescaut: His first great success, in 1893, based on the same story as Massenet's Manon. It made Puccini Italy's rising star.
Operas by Puccini.Il tabarro: A grim one-act set on a Seine barge, and the first part of Puccini's Il trittico. A husband murders his wife's lover.
Operas by Puccini.Suor Angelica: The middle panel of Il trittico, set in a convent, with an all-female cast. Puccini said it was his favorite of his own operas.
Operas by Puccini.La rondine: A lighter 1917 work about a Parisian courtesan, often called Puccini's operetta-like piece. It is rarely staged.
Operas by Puccini.Aida: Verdi's opera set in ancient Egypt. It premiered in Cairo in 1871, and its Triumphal March often uses real trumpets.
Operas by Puccini.La Traviata: Verdi's 1853 opera about the courtesan Violetta, adapted from Dumas fils's The Lady of the Camellias. It was not by Puccini.
Operas by Puccini.Rigoletto: Verdi's opera about a hunchbacked court jester. Its tune La donna è mobile was kept secret until opening night to prevent leaks.
Operas by Puccini.Carmen: Bizet's French opera about a free-spirited cigarette factory worker in Seville. The Habanera is one of its most famous tunes.
Operas by Puccini.Otello: Verdi's late-career Shakespeare adaptation, premiered in 1887. It is Verdi, not Puccini, who composed this tragedy.
Operas by Puccini.Nabucco: Verdi's 1842 breakthrough, and its chorus Va, pensiero became a patriotic hymn of Italian unification. Verdi wrote it, not Puccini.
Operas by Puccini.Don Giovanni: Mozart's 1787 opera about a seducer dragged to hell by a stone statue. It is a Mozart opera, not Puccini's.
Operas by Puccini.The Magic Flute: Mozart's 1791 German-language opera, with the Queen of the Night's famously high coloratura aria. Not by Puccini.
Operas by Puccini.Norma: Bellini's 1831 opera about a Druid priestess. Its aria Casta diva is a famously difficult piece for sopranos.
Operas by Puccini.Pagliacci: Leoncavallo's 1892 opera about a clown who murders his wife on stage. It is often paired with Cavalleria rusticana, but it isn't Puccini's.
Operas by Puccini.Cavalleria rusticana: Mascagni's one-act verismo opera from 1890. Its Intermezzo was used in Raging Bull's opening, but it isn't Puccini's.
Operas by Puccini.Lucia di Lammermoor: Donizetti's 1835 tragedy, famous for the mad scene. It was often sung with a glass harmonica in the original version.
Operas by Puccini.Fidelio: Beethoven's only opera, about a wife who disguises herself to rescue her husband. It took him three versions to satisfy himself.
Operas by Puccini.Lakmé: Delibes's 1883 opera set in British India. The Flower Duet from it is widely used in advertising, but it isn't Puccini.
Operas by Puccini.Barber of Seville: Rossini's 1816 comic opera. Its premiere was disrupted by a cat on stage and a rowdy audience of supporters of a rival composer.

Madonna songs.Like a Virgin: Her 1984 VMA performance in a wedding dress, rolling on the stage floor, helped make this her first US number one.
Madonna songs.Like a Prayer: The 1989 video's burning crosses and stigmata led Pepsi to cancel a huge ad deal with her, but the song stayed a classic.
Madonna songs.Vogue: Named for a dance from New York's Harlem ballroom scene, it lists Hollywood stars in a rap and sold millions worldwide.
Madonna songs.Material Girl: The video recreates Marilyn Monroe's pink gown scene from Gentlemen Prefer Blondes, a nod to the film's Diamonds Are a Girl's Best Friend.
Madonna songs.Holiday: Her 1983 breakthrough, first US top-ten hit, was written by Curtis Hudson and Lisa Stevens, and it's still a pure party anthem.
Madonna songs.La Isla Bonita: She reportedly got it after Michael Jackson passed on it. The Spanish-flavoured track became a worldwide hit in 1987.
Madonna songs.Papa Don't Preach: A 1986 song about teen pregnancy that sparked heated debate, with groups praising and condemning its message.
Madonna songs.Express Yourself: The 1989 video was inspired by Fritz Lang's film Metropolis, and was one of the priciest music videos made then.
Madonna songs.Frozen: The 1998 video, directed by Chris Cunningham, sees her turn into a flock of ravens in a desert.
Madonna songs.Music: Her 2000 hit built on vocoder-twisted vocals by producer Mirwais, which helped define her reinvention that year.
Madonna songs.Hung Up: Samples ABBA's Gimme! Gimme! Gimme!, and Guinness recorded it topping the charts in 41 countries.
Madonna songs.Into the Groove: Featured in Desperately Seeking Susan, it was only a B-side in the US, but became her first UK number one.
Madonna songs.Ray of Light: The title track of her 1998 album, produced by William Orbit, won her Grammys and signalled an electronic reinvention.
Madonna songs.Time After Time: Cyndi Lauper's 1984 ballad. Madonna's era-mate, but Lauper's song, later covered by Miles Davis.
Madonna songs.Like a Rolling Stone: Bob Dylan's 1965 classic. Madonna's Like a Prayer shares the 'like a' structure, hence the trap.
Madonna songs.Wannabe: The Spice Girls' 1996 debut single, whose 'zig-a-zig-ah' hook became one of the best-known in pop.
Madonna songs.Toxic: Britney Spears's 2004 hit, whose looping Bollywood-style strings sample comes from a Bollywood tune.
Madonna songs.Believe: Cher's 1998 hit made Auto-Tune famous, and was a huge comeback for the singer at age 52.
Madonna songs.Bad Romance: Lady Gaga's 2009 hit. Gaga often draws comparisons to Madonna, but this isn't hers.
Madonna songs.Purple Rain: Prince's 1984 title track. Madonna and Prince were rivals-turned-collaborators on her Like a Prayer album, but the song is Prince's.
Madonna songs.Billie Jean: Michael Jackson's 1982 hit, based on a stalker story and driven by a famous bassline.
Madonna songs.Physical: Olivia Newton-John's 1981 hit, which spent 10 weeks at number one in the US and had a gym-themed video.
Madonna songs.Call Me: Blondie's 1980 hit, produced by Giorgio Moroder for the film American Gigolo.
Madonna songs.Heart of Glass: Blondie's 1979 disco-rock hit, which started life as a reggae-flavoured song called The Disco Song.

Sports and martial arts from Japan.Judo: Founded in 1882 by Jigoro Kano, its name means gentle way. In 1964 it became the first Asian martial art in the Olympics.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Karate: Means empty hand and developed in Okinawa. It made its Olympic debut at the Tokyo Games.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Sumo: Wrestlers throw salt to purify the ring. A yokozuna, the top rank, can never be demoted, only retire.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Kendo: Fencing with bamboo swords and body armour. A strike only scores if it comes with a shout and proper form.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Aikido: Created by Morihei Ueshiba in the early 20th century. It aims to redirect an attacker's momentum rather than meet force with force.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Jujutsu: A samurai-era grappling art that inspired Brazilian jiu-jitsu, which Mitsuyo Maeda taught in Brazil.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Kyudo: Japanese archery with an asymmetric bow over two metres long. Form and spirit matter as much as hitting the target.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Keirin: Created for betting in 1948, where riders follow a pacing motorbike that peels off before the sprint. Olympic since 2000.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Iaido: The art of drawing a sword, cutting and sheathing it in one flowing movement, practised alone against an imagined opponent.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Taekwondo: Korean in origin, and the name means the way of the foot and fist.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Kung fu: Chinese, and the term loosely means skill achieved through hard work.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Tai chi: Chinese, a slow flowing practice that began as a martial art.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Muay Thai: Thailand's art of eight limbs, striking with fists, elbows, knees and shins.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Capoeira: An Afro-Brazilian art disguised as dance. UNESCO lists it as intangible cultural heritage.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Krav Maga: Developed in Israel by Imi Lichtenfeld for military self-defence.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Wing Chun: Chinese, and taught by Ip Man, who in turn taught Bruce Lee.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Hapkido: Korean, blending joint locks, throws and kicks.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Silat: A family of fighting arts from the Malay world in Southeast Asia.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Sepak takraw: Southeast Asian, like volleyball played with the feet and a woven rattan ball.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Kabaddi: Indian, where raiders must chant the name in one breath while tagging opponents.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Wushu: China's modern martial arts sport, judged on forms or contact.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Sambo: Soviet, developed in the 1930s for the Red Army.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Savate: French kickboxing, where fighters wear shoes and strike with the foot.
Sports and martial arts from Japan.Jeet Kune Do: Bruce Lee's own philosophy, whose name means the way of the intercepting fist.

Things that don't belong in the fridge.Shoes: Shoes in the fridge is a gag, but cold shoes would be stiff, and shoes need airflow to dry out.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.TV remote: A TV remote left in the fridge is a classic sign of forgetfulness, and its batteries lose power faster in the cold.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Socks: Socks in the fridge would pick up odors, and the fridge door is among the dirtiest, warmest spots inside it.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Laptop: A laptop in the fridge could get condensation damage once taken out into warm air, so it is a bad place for one.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Keys: Keys in the fridge are a famous sign of a distracted mind, and the cold does not harm them.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Books: Books in a fridge would absorb moisture and warp, since paper stays best in a dry, room-temperature place.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Toothbrush: A toothbrush should dry in open air, since a cold, damp fridge would encourage bacteria and does nothing for it.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Wallet: A wallet in the fridge is a joke, but leather would stiffen in the cold and any cards or cash could get damp.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Houseplant: Most houseplants come from the tropics, and a fridge's dark cold would kill them quickly, so keep them by a window.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Sweater: Wool sweaters should be stored dry and clean, since the damp inside a fridge would invite mold, and moths avoid cold anyway.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Hairbrush: A hairbrush in the fridge makes no sense, since cold does nothing to help it work, and it belongs in the bathroom.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Milk: Milk is kept cold because bacteria multiply quickly above about 4 degrees Celsius, and pasteurization only slows spoilage.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Eggs: In the US, eggs are washed and refrigerated, but in much of Europe they are not washed and are stored on the counter.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Butter: Butter is fine on the counter for a day or two in a covered dish, and the fridge only extends its life.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Cheese: Cheese is kept cold for storage, but most cheeses taste best if you let them warm up for a half hour first.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Yogurt: Yogurt contains live bacteria cultures, and the cold of the fridge keeps them slow and the product safe to eat.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Leftovers: Leftovers should reach the fridge within about two hours, and most are good for three to four days.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Orange juice: Orange juice keeps its flavor and vitamin C much longer when stored cold, so it does belong in the fridge.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Lettuce: Lettuce is about 95 percent water, and it wilts fast, so a cold crisper drawer keeps it crisp.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Ham: Cured ham keeps well in the fridge, and the curing process with salt dates back thousands of years.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Mayonnaise: Mayonnaise is acidic, which helps hold back germs, and it only needs the fridge after opening.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Salsa: Fresh salsa is full of fresh tomato and onion, so it belongs in the fridge, and it keeps only a week or so.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Cream: Cream is milkfat that rises to the top of milk, and it whips best when both the cream and the bowl are very cold.
Things that don't belong in the fridge.Hot dogs: Hot dogs are precooked but still need the fridge, and an opened pack should be eaten within about a week.

Words for a business owner.Entrepreneur: The word is French, meaning one who undertakes, and the economist Richard Cantillon helped popularize it in the 1700s.
Words for a business owner.Proprietor: It comes from the Latin for property, and is a slightly old-fashioned word for the owner of a shop, pub or hotel.
Words for a business owner.Founder: It suggests someone who started the business, and many famous firms, like Apple, began in a garage or a family home.
Words for a business owner.Owner: The simplest term; in many countries a sole owner is personally responsible for all the business debts.
Words for a business owner.Tycoon: It comes from the Japanese "taikun", a title meaning great lord, and was later brought into English for powerful businesspeople.
Words for a business owner.Magnate: From the Latin for great person, it was used for nobles in medieval Poland and Hungary before it meant a business giant.
Words for a business owner.Mogul: It originally meant a Mughal emperor of India, and Hollywood later borrowed it for the powerful heads of movie studios.
Words for a business owner.Industrialist: Industrialists such as Andrew Carnegie built huge factories in the 1800s, and many later became famous donors.
Words for a business owner.Shopkeeper: Napoleon is said to have called England a nation of shopkeepers, though he may have taken the phrase from Adam Smith.
Words for a business owner.Restaurateur: The word has no letter n in its middle, which is a common slip; it comes from French, from restaurer, to restore.
Words for a business owner.Employee: An employee works for the owner rather than owning, though many companies give staff shares so they become part-owners too.
Words for a business owner.Intern: The word began in medicine for doctors in training who lived in the hospital, and the name came from French for internal.
Words for a business owner.Customer: The word came from Old French for someone who regularly buys, a habit that makes them the lifeblood of any owner.
Words for a business owner.Client: In ancient Rome a client was a person under the protection of a wealthy patron, long before lawyers had clients.
Words for a business owner.Tenant: A tenant rents space from the owner, and the word is Latin for holding, so a business owner can be a tenant too.
Words for a business owner.Consumer: It is a person who uses up goods; in business economics, consumer spending drives about two thirds of the US economy.
Words for a business owner.Shopper: Studies show most shoppers turn right after entering a shop, so stores often put the key displays on that side.
Words for a business owner.Apprentice: Guild apprentices in the Middle Ages trained for years, often seven, before becoming journeymen, who then aimed to own a shop.
Words for a business owner.Trainee: A trainee is learning on the job under the owner, which is a stage before running a business, not the owner.
Words for a business owner.Subordinate: The word means placed below in rank, from the Latin sub for under, so it is the opposite of the boss.
Words for a business owner.Clerk: The word comes from "cleric", since in the Middle Ages the few people who could read and write were churchmen.
Words for a business owner.Guest: Guest and host come from the same ancient root, so the very word that names a visitor is related to the one who welcomes.
Words for a business owner.Lodger: A lodger rents a room in someone's home, so is a paying resident, not an owner of the business.
Words for a business owner.Passenger: The word comes from the French for passing, and passengers pay for transport but do not own the carrier.

Things a librarian works with.Library cards: Library cards were once paper cards. A borrower's name was written in a ledger or stamped into the book's own card.
Things a librarian works with.Book cart: A book cart is a trolley librarians use to reshelve returns. Library staff even compete in book-cart drill teams.
Things a librarian works with.Date stamp: Date stamps once marked every due date in the back of a book, but barcodes and computers have mostly replaced them.
Things a librarian works with.Catalog: Libraries once kept drawers of paper index cards, but online catalogs, called OPACs, took over from about the 1980s.
Things a librarian works with.Barcode scanner: Scanners link each book's barcode to a record, so checkout takes a second. The first retail barcode ever scanned was on a pack of gum in 1974.
Things a librarian works with.Returns slot: Returns slots let you drop off books after hours, and many drop into a padded bin to protect them.
Things a librarian works with.Shelving: Shelving takes up much of a librarian's day, since a book put on the wrong shelf is almost as good as lost forever.
Things a librarian works with.Reading lists: Librarians compile reading lists to point readers toward the next good book, a way of making the huge shelves less daunting.
Things a librarian works with.Interlibrary loans: Interlibrary loan lets libraries lend books to each other, so your local branch can get you a book held far away.
Things a librarian works with.Dewey Decimal: Melvil Dewey published his decimal system in 1876. It sorts all knowledge into ten main classes, from 000 to 900.
Things a librarian works with.Bookends: Bookends hold up rows of books so they don't slump. A librarian's small tool to keep the shelves tidy.
Things a librarian works with.Stethoscope: A stethoscope is a doctor's tool for listening to the heart. A librarian listens for whispers instead.
Things a librarian works with.Anvil: An anvil is the iron block on which blacksmiths hammer metal. A library's heavy hitters are encyclopedias, not anvils.
Things a librarian works with.Saddle: Saddles belong on horses. There is no library job that involves one, though bookmobiles used to ride around.
Things a librarian works with.Pitchfork: A pitchfork is a farm tool. Librarians use sorting carts, not pitchforks, for tossing hay.
Things a librarian works with.Kiln: A kiln fires clay in a potter's studio. A library is kept cool and dry to preserve its books.
Things a librarian works with.Fishing rod: A fishing rod belongs by a lake. The only fishing at a library is looking for a lost title, using the catalog.
Things a librarian works with.Paint roller: A paint roller covers walls quickly. Librarians avoid wet paint near books, since moisture damages paper.
Things a librarian works with.Hacksaw: A hacksaw cuts through metal in a workshop. Librarians cut nothing, except maybe a late fine for good readers.
Things a librarian works with.Lasso: A lasso is a cowboy's rope with a sliding loop for catching cattle. Library books are returned, not roped in.
Things a librarian works with.Jackhammer: A jackhammer breaks up pavement with a deafening racket, the opposite of a library's famously quiet reading room.
Things a librarian works with.Gavel: A gavel is a judge's or auctioneer's mallet. A librarian's way to call for quiet is a pointed look or a shush.
Things a librarian works with.Plunger: A plunger clears blocked drains. A librarian's version is clearing a jammed returns slot, which isn't the same tool.
Things a librarian works with.Welding torch: A welding torch melts metal with a flame hotter than 3,000 degrees Celsius, an obvious hazard in a building full of paper.

Jobs at a museum.Curator: The word comes from the Latin for care, and a curator chooses, researches and cares for a collection and decides what goes on display.
Jobs at a museum.Conservator: Conservators stabilize and restore artifacts using chemistry and microscopes, aiming for repairs that can be undone later.
Jobs at a museum.Docent: Typically a trained volunteer, the docent leads visitors through the galleries; the term comes from the Latin docere, to teach.
Jobs at a museum.Archivist: Archivists keep records, letters and photographs, and a large museum may hold far more in storage than it ever shows.
Jobs at a museum.Security guard: Museums rely heavily on guards, but the 1990 Isabella Stewart Gardner heist in Boston, still unsolved, was pulled off by thieves in police uniforms.
Jobs at a museum.Tour guide: Guides turn a collection into a story; a good one knows which objects are most popular and how to avoid the crowds around them.
Jobs at a museum.Exhibit designer: They decide the lighting, labels and layout, and carefully control light levels because it can fade old textiles and paper.
Jobs at a museum.Gift shop clerk: Museum shops often fund the institution and can bring in a large share of the income that keeps the place running.
Jobs at a museum.Taxidermist: Natural history museums employ them to prepare specimens; the preserved skins of animals are often decades or centuries old.
Jobs at a museum.Sommelier: This wine expert works in restaurants, where the Court of Master Sommeliers sets a famously hard exam, not in galleries.
Jobs at a museum.Bellhop: Bellhops carry luggage in hotels; the job gets its name from the bell that guests rang for service.
Jobs at a museum.Croupier: The casino dealer's title comes from the French for the person who stands behind a gambler to support him, from croupe, the rump.
Jobs at a museum.Lifeguard: Lifeguards watch pools and beaches; a museum would only need one if it had an indoor pool, which is rare.
Jobs at a museum.Midwife: Midwives help with childbirth, and the word means with woman in Old English, so it belongs in a hospital.
Jobs at a museum.Jockey: Jockeys ride racehorses, often weighing under 120 pounds, and don't turn up at museums except as part of an exhibit.
Jobs at a museum.Shepherd: The job is thousands of years old and appears in many ancient texts, but it takes place in pastures rather than galleries.
Jobs at a museum.Lumberjack: Lumberjacks fell trees in forests; a few museums dedicated to logging exist, though the workers themselves don't staff them.
Jobs at a museum.Air marshal: Armed federal officers sit undercover on flights, and a museum isn't a place where you'd find one on duty.
Jobs at a museum.Golf caddie: Caddies carry clubs and give advice on the course; the word comes from the French cadet, a young soldier.
Jobs at a museum.Gondolier: Venice's gondoliers must pass a demanding licensing process, and the city allows only a few hundred of them.
Jobs at a museum.Farrier: A farrier shoes horses and trims their hooves, a skilled trade, but one that belongs at stables and not at museums.
Jobs at a museum.Bailiff: Bailiffs keep order in courtrooms and enforce judgments; the job has medieval English roots.
Jobs at a museum.Coal miner: Coal mining is dangerous underground labor, though mining museums often employ former miners as guides.
Jobs at a museum.Chimney sweep: Sweeps were once boys sent up narrow flues, and Victorian reforms banned the practice of climbing boys.

Handheld game consoles.Game Boy: Its 1989 launch bundled Tetris, and the grey brick with a murky green screen went on to sell over a hundred million units with its successors.
Handheld game consoles.Game Gear: Sega's 1990 answer to Game Boy had a backlit color screen, but it gobbled six AA batteries in just a few hours of play.
Handheld game consoles.PSP: Sony's first handheld played games on tiny UMD discs and sold roughly 80 million units, a strong showing against Nintendo's DS.
Handheld game consoles.PS Vita: Launched in 2011 with an OLED screen and two analog sticks, it was hampered by pricey proprietary memory cards.
Handheld game consoles.Nintendo DS: The name means Dual Screen; its touch screen and microphone helped it sell over 150 million units, among the best-selling consoles ever.
Handheld game consoles.3DS: It showed 3D without glasses using a parallax barrier, and a slider let players dial the effect down or switch it off entirely.
Handheld game consoles.Atari Lynx: Released in 1989, this was the first color handheld, and its screen could be flipped upside down so left-handed players were comfortable.
Handheld game consoles.Game Boy Advance: Its 2001 debut kept backward compatibility with Game Boy and Game Boy Color cartridges, so players' old libraries still worked.
Handheld game consoles.Steam Deck: Valve's 2022 handheld is a portable PC running a Linux-based system, so with a little tinkering it can even act as a desktop computer.
Handheld game consoles.Switch Lite: Unlike the regular Switch, this 2019 model cannot connect to a TV, because its controllers are built permanently into the body.
Handheld game consoles.N-Gage: Nokia's 2003 phone-console hybrid had to be held sideways to make calls, earning the mocking nickname 'taco phone'.
Handheld game consoles.Neo Geo Pocket: SNK's 1998 handheld had a famously clicky joystick, yet it was discontinued by 2000 as Game Boy Color dominated the market.
Handheld game consoles.GameCube: A home console, though its small cube shape and built-in carry handle tempted many to treat it like a portable. It needed a TV.
Handheld game consoles.Dreamcast: Sega's last console was home-only, but its memory card, the VMU, had its own tiny screen and could play mini-games alone.
Handheld game consoles.Xbox: Microsoft's first console was a TV machine with a built-in hard drive, which was unusual for consoles at the time.
Handheld game consoles.PS2: The best-selling console ever, at over 150 million units, but strictly a home system that needed a TV and a wall socket.
Handheld game consoles.Wii: A TV console through and through, though its motion controller was the star; its Wii U successor's tablet screen was the closest it got to portable.
Handheld game consoles.Nintendo 64: Plugs into a TV, famous for its three-pronged controller and four ports for local multiplayer.
Handheld game consoles.SNES: A home console, but its games now travel: Nintendo's online service lets Switch owners, including Lite users, play SNES classics on the go.
Handheld game consoles.Genesis: Sega did make a handheld Genesis, the 1995 Nomad, but the Genesis itself was a TV console.
Handheld game consoles.Atari 2600: A 1977 home console whose wood-grain panel was a deliberate nod to living-room furniture, so it blended in.
Handheld game consoles.Saturn: A home console whose dual-CPU design was notoriously hard to program, one reason it lost ground to PlayStation.
Handheld game consoles.PS5: A home console, though Sony's Portal accessory can stream its games to a handheld screen over Wi-Fi.
Handheld game consoles.Xbox 360: A home console whose 'red ring of death' hardware failures cost Microsoft over a billion dollars in repairs.

AI research companies.OpenAI: Founded in 2015 as a nonprofit, it released ChatGPT in 2022 and had over 100 million users within about two months.
AI research companies.Anthropic: Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI staff, it makes the Claude models and describes itself as a safety-focused AI lab.
AI research companies.DeepMind: Founded in London in 2010 and bought by Google in 2014, its AlphaGo beat a top Go player in 2016 and AlphaFold predicted protein structures.
AI research companies.Mistral: A Paris startup founded in 2023 by former DeepMind and Meta researchers, known for releasing open-weight models.
AI research companies.xAI: Elon Musk founded it in 2023, and its Grok chatbot is built into the X platform.
AI research companies.Hugging Face: Named after an emoji, it began as a teen chatbot app and became the main hub for sharing open AI models.
AI research companies.Midjourney: This image generator, launched in 2022, became famous because users prompt it through Discord.
AI research companies.Stability AI: Its Stable Diffusion model, released openly in 2022, let anyone run an AI image generator at home.
AI research companies.Cohere: This Toronto company was co-founded by Aidan Gomez, a co-author of the 2017 paper that introduced the Transformer.
AI research companies.Perplexity: Launched in 2022 as an AI answer engine that cites sources, it positioned itself as an alternative to traditional search.
AI research companies.Netflix: Netflix uses AI for recommendations but is a streaming company, not an AI research lab; it started by mailing DVDs.
AI research companies.Spotify: The Swedish streamer relies on machine learning for playlists, but it is a music service, not a research lab.
AI research companies.Dropbox: Drew Houston started it after repeatedly forgetting his USB drive; it is a storage company.
AI research companies.Zoom: Its use exploded during the 2020 pandemic; it makes video software, not AI research.
AI research companies.Uber: Originally called UberCab, it was launched in San Francisco in 2009 as a ride-hailing company.
AI research companies.Airbnb: It began in 2008 when the founders rented out air mattresses on their apartment floor, and it is a travel marketplace.
AI research companies.Shopify: The Canadian e-commerce platform began as an online snowboard shop called Snowdevil.
AI research companies.Etsy: A marketplace for handmade and vintage goods founded in 2005, not an AI research company.
AI research companies.Pinterest: Its visual bookmarking service launched in 2010; it's social media, not an AI lab.
AI research companies.Peloton: Known for connected exercise bikes, it is a fitness company, despite its tech branding.
AI research companies.Roku: It makes streaming devices and a TV platform; it's a media company, not an AI lab.
AI research companies.GoPro: Founder Nick Woodman first strapped cameras to his wrist while surfing; they make action cameras.
AI research companies.Lyft: It started as Zimride, a long-distance carpooling service, and became a ride-hailing rival to Uber.
AI research companies.DoorDash: It began as PaloAltoDelivery.com, a Stanford student project, and is a food delivery company.

Characters in Hamlet.Hamlet: The prince delays avenging his father, and he speaks over a third of the lines, making him Shakespeare's biggest role.
Characters in Hamlet.Ophelia: Her drowning is among the most painted scenes in literature, most famously by John Everett Millais.
Characters in Hamlet.Polonius: He advises 'to thine own self be true', and Hamlet stabs him through a tapestry, mistaking him for the king.
Characters in Hamlet.Laertes: Ophelia's brother duels Hamlet with a poisoned blade, and his grief for his father and sister mirrors Hamlet's own.
Characters in Hamlet.Horatio: Hamlet's loyal friend is one of the few survivors, and he is left to tell the story.
Characters in Hamlet.Gertrude: Hamlet's mother marries her dead husband's brother soon after the funeral, which disgusts her son.
Characters in Hamlet.Claudius: He murdered the old king by pouring poison in his ear, and Hamlet stages a play to catch his guilt.
Characters in Hamlet.Rosencrantz: Hamlet's schoolfriend is sent to spy on him, and he became a star of Tom Stoppard's play about him and Guildenstern.
Characters in Hamlet.Guildenstern: He and Rosencrantz are sent to deliver Hamlet to his death in England, and are cleverly sent to their deaths instead.
Characters in Hamlet.Yorick: The dead court jester whose skull Hamlet holds in the graveyard is the play's best-known image of mortality.
Characters in Hamlet.Fortinbras: Norway's prince marches into Denmark at the end and takes the crown after the court lies dead.
Characters in Hamlet.Osric: A fussy courtier who sets up the fencing match that proves fatal for Hamlet and most of the royal family.
Characters in Hamlet.Iago: Iago is the scheming villain in Othello, so he comes from a different Shakespearean tragedy.
Characters in Hamlet.Desdemona: Othello's wife, whose lost handkerchief is a key prop in that play, not in Hamlet.
Characters in Hamlet.Banquo: Banquo's ghost haunts Macbeth's banquet; he is a Scottish nobleman, not a Danish one.
Characters in Hamlet.Macduff: The Scottish thane who kills Macbeth belongs to a different tragedy.
Characters in Hamlet.Puck: A mischievous fairy in A Midsummer Night's Dream, far from the gloomy castle at Elsinore.
Characters in Hamlet.Prospero: The exiled duke and magician of The Tempest, not from Hamlet.
Characters in Hamlet.Miranda: Prospero's daughter in The Tempest has grown up seeing almost no one except her father, so she isn't in Hamlet.
Characters in Hamlet.Mercutio: Romeo's witty friend who dies cursing both families belongs to Romeo and Juliet.
Characters in Hamlet.Tybalt: Juliet's hot-tempered cousin, nicknamed the Prince of Cats, belongs to Romeo and Juliet.
Characters in Hamlet.Cordelia: King Lear's honest youngest daughter belongs to a different tragedy.
Characters in Hamlet.Portia: She is the clever heroine of The Merchant of Venice, who disguises herself as a lawyer.
Characters in Hamlet.Shylock: The moneylender of The Merchant of Venice, who demands a pound of flesh, is not at Elsinore.

Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Curse: Verse and curse are a textbook rhyme, though in the Bible and in poetry they often appear together.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Purse: Rhymes with verse; the old saying warns you can't make a silk one from a sow's ear.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Nurse: Rhymes with verse; from Latin 'nutrire', to nourish, since the original nurse was a wet nurse who fed a baby.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Hearse: Rhymes with verse; it began as a triangular frame for candles at funerals, from a Latin word for a harrow, before it meant a car.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Worse: 'Worse' comes from Old English and is the irregular comparative of bad, ending with the same sound as verse.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Terse: Rhymes with verse; from Latin 'tersus', wiped clean, as in a reply stripped down to almost nothing.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Rehearse: Shares a root with 'hearse': both trace to the French for a harrow, meaning to rake over again.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Universe: The stress falls on the first syllable (YOO-ni-verse), so the ending lines up with verse; the word comes from Latin for 'turned into one'.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Reverse: Rhymes with verse, and comes from Latin for turning back; a coin's flip side is its reverse.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Disperse: Rhymes with verse; the Latin root means to scatter in different directions, like seeds or a crowd.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Immerse: Rhymes with verse; from Latin for dipping into, as when a diver or a language learner is fully immersed.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Converse: Rhymes with verse as a verb meaning to talk; as a noun meaning 'the opposite' it shifts stress to the first syllable.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Horse: It looks close, but it is pronounced with an 'or' vowel, so it rhymes with force, not verse.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Force: Rhymes with horse and force, not verse; the spelling looks similar, but the vowel is the 'or' sound.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Course: Rhymes with horse and force, not verse; the 'or' vowel here is not the 'ur' of verse.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Hoarse: A homophone of horse, so it rhymes with force and course, but not with verse; the word describes a rough, raspy voice.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Fierce: Has the 'ear' sound, so it rhymes with pierce and tears, not with verse, despite the similar r and s endings.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Nurture: Its first syllable sounds like verse, but the word ends in 'chur', so it fails to rhyme; it comes from Latin for nourishing.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".First: Almost rhymes with verse, but the extra t at the end (as in 'burst' and 'first') makes it only a near rhyme.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Thirst: A near rhyme with 'verse' that adds a t before the end; the s sound is missing at the end.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Mercy: It begins with the same vowel sound as verse but ends in 'see', so only the opening is similar; it comes from Latin for wages or reward.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Worth: Ends with th rather than s, so it only half-rhymes with verse; the word goes back to Old English 'weorth'.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Herb: In American English it is 'urb', close to verse but ending in b, which kills the rhyme.
Words that rhyme with \"verse\".Birth: Ends with the th sound, not s, so it is a near rhyme at best; it comes from Old English and shares roots with 'bear'.

Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Raven: Published in 1845, it made Poe famous almost overnight, though he reportedly earned only about $9 for it. Its refrain is "Nevermore".
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Annabel Lee: Poe's last complete poem, published just after his death in 1849. Many readers hear in it an echo of his young wife Virginia, who died of tuberculosis.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Tell-Tale Heart: A narrator insists he is perfectly sane while describing a murder, then cracks when he imagines the dead man's heart still beating under the floor.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Black Cat: A man's drinking and cruelty toward his pet cat end in murder, and a second cat's wail from behind a wall finally gives him away.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Gold-Bug: A treasure hunt solved by a cipher, it won Poe a $100 newspaper prize in 1843 and helped spark a public craze for cryptograms.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Bells: Poe's poem imitates its subject: the rhythm and repeated words ring like sleigh, wedding, alarm and funeral bells, growing darker with each stanza.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Lenore: The lost beloved mourned in "The Raven", and also the title of a separate Poe poem about a dead maiden that he revised several times.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Eldorado: Poe's late poem about a knight who spends his life seeking the legendary golden land and learns it lies beyond the grave, "over the Mountains of the Moon".
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Oval Portrait: A wounded traveler reads about a painter whose young wife wastes away as her portrait grows more lifelike, until the last brushstroke is her death.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Ligeia: Poe called it his best tale: a widower is haunted by his first wife, who seems to return by taking over the body of his second.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Purloined Letter: The third of Poe's Dupin detective stories. The stolen letter is found hidden in plain sight, in a card rack, because Dupin knows nobody looks there.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Dracula: Bram Stoker's novel of 1897, written decades after Poe died in 1849. Vampire fans may wish it were his, but it isn't.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Frankenstein: Mary Shelley wrote it in 1818, aged about twenty, after a ghost-story contest with Lord Byron and Percy Shelley. Not Poe.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Monkey's Paw: W. W. Jacobs's 1902 tale of three wishes and their dreadful price feels like Poe, but it was written by an English author.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Carmilla: Sheridan Le Fanu's 1872 vampire novella predates Dracula by 25 years. It has a Gothic Poe mood but is not by Poe.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Invisible Man: H. G. Wells's 1897 science-fiction novel about a scientist who turns himself transparent. Poe never wrote it.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Sleepy Hollow: Washington Irving's 1820 story of Ichabod Crane and the Headless Horseman is American Gothic, but Irving wrote it, not Poe.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Rip Van Winkle: Washington Irving's tale of a man who sleeps for twenty years in the Catskills and wakes to a new country. Irving, not Poe.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Yellow Wallpaper: Charlotte Perkins Gilman's 1892 story of a woman driven mad by a "rest cure". It's a classic of feminist horror, but not by Poe.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Lottery: Shirley Jackson's 1948 story of a village ritual drew a flood of angry letters when The New Yorker printed it. Not Poe.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Signal-Man: Charles Dickens's 1866 ghost story, about a railway signalman haunted by warnings of disaster, is eerie enough to pass as Poe but isn't.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.The Birds: Daphne du Maurier's 1952 story, later filmed by Hitchcock in 1963. A hostile bird tale, but the Poe bird is a raven.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Jabberwocky: Lewis Carroll's nonsense poem from Through the Looking-Glass. Poe's strangeness is darker, and Carroll wrote this one.
Works by Edgar Allan Poe.Kubla Khan: Coleridge's 1797 opium-dream poem, left unfinished, he said, when a visitor interrupted him. A dreamy fragment, not Poe.

Characters in Watership Down.Hazel: Richard Adams first told the story to his daughters on a car trip, and Hazel leads the escape.
Characters in Watership Down.Fiver: Fiver is the runt whose prophetic visions of doom push Hazel's group to leave their warren.
Characters in Watership Down.Bigwig: Bigwig is the strong former officer of the Owsla who joins the group and infiltrates the tyrannical Efrafa.
Characters in Watership Down.Blackberry: Blackberry is the clever rabbit who comes up with ideas like using a boat to cross the river.
Characters in Watership Down.Dandelion: Dandelion is fast and a good storyteller, reciting tales of the trickster hero El-ahrairah to keep spirits up.
Characters in Watership Down.Pipkin: Pipkin is a tiny, timid rabbit who is Fiver's friend and, like him, loved by Hazel.
Characters in Watership Down.Kehaar: The injured black-headed gull speaks in broken English and helps the rabbits.
Characters in Watership Down.General Woundwort: General Woundwort is the scarred tyrant of Efrafa, a warren run like a military state, who hunts escapees.
Characters in Watership Down.Holly: Holly is a captain of the Owsla of the Sandleford warren, wounded when he escapes, and returns later.
Characters in Watership Down.Silver: Silver is another Sandleford rabbit who survives the warren's destruction and joins Hazel's warren.
Characters in Watership Down.Cowslip: Cowslip leads a strange warren fed by farmers, where the rabbits hide the truth about snares.
Characters in Watership Down.Peter Rabbit: Peter Rabbit, Beatrix Potter's naughty rabbit in a blue jacket, raids Mr. McGregor's garden, but he isn't in Watership Down.
Characters in Watership Down.Benjamin Bunny: Benjamin Bunny is Peter Rabbit's cousin in Beatrix Potter's tales, set in an English garden rather than on the down.
Characters in Watership Down.Thumper: Thumper is the foot-thumping rabbit friend of Bambi in Disney's film, not a member of Hazel's warren.
Characters in Watership Down.Brer Rabbit: Brer Rabbit is the trickster of African American folk tales collected by Joel Chandler Harris, not from Watership Down.
Characters in Watership Down.Bugs Bunny: Bugs Bunny is the 'What's up, Doc?' star of Warner Bros cartoons, with no part in Watership Down.
Characters in Watership Down.White Rabbit: The White Rabbit hurries by in Wonderland, where Alice follows him, and is not from Richard Adams's tale.
Characters in Watership Down.March Hare: The March Hare is a hare, not a rabbit, and hosts the mad tea party in Alice in Wonderland.
Characters in Watership Down.Roger Rabbit: Roger Rabbit, the cartoon star of Who Framed Roger Rabbit, is a film creation, not from Adams's book.
Characters in Watership Down.Flopsy: Flopsy is one of Peter Rabbit's well-behaved sisters in Beatrix Potter's story.
Characters in Watership Down.Velveteen Rabbit: The Velveteen Rabbit is a toy rabbit who longs to become real in Margery Williams's 1922 story.
Characters in Watership Down.Miffy: Miffy is Dutch artist Dick Bruna's little white rabbit, created in 1955.
Characters in Watership Down.Harvey: Harvey is the invisible six-foot rabbit friend of Elwood P. Dowd, played in the film by James Stewart.
Characters in Watership Down.Peter Cottontail: Peter Cottontail is the Easter bunny of song, hopping down the bunny trail, and not from Adams's book.

Things with handles.Coffee mug: The handle matters physically: it lets you hold a hot drink without touching the ceramic, which is why mugs began as heavy tankards.
Things with handles.Suitcase: Wheeled suitcases only appeared in 1970 and took decades to catch on, partly because travelers thought rolling them seemed unmanly.
Things with handles.Door: Door handles are among the dirtiest surfaces in buildings, and copper handles kill many germs on contact.
Things with handles.Frying pan: Pan handles are often hollow stainless or cast iron so they stay cooler, though cast iron ones heat right up.
Things with handles.Bucket: The bail, a bucket's wire handle, pivots so the bucket can hang from a hook or swing while it's full.
Things with handles.Umbrella: Umbrella handles come hooked or straight, and the hook form lets it hang on your arm or a chair.
Things with handles.Hammer: A hammer's handle was traditionally hickory or ash because those woods absorb shock and are tough but flexible.
Things with handles.Teapot: A teapot's handle sits opposite the spout so the pour balances, and some old ones were made with a gap to stay cooler.
Things with handles.Briefcase: Briefcases began as bags carrying legal briefs, and their name still reflects that origin.
Things with handles.Kettle: Kettle handles are often plastic because metal would be dangerously hot, and 'put the kettle on' is a British ritual.
Things with handles.Scissors: Scissors have two handles, called bows, and they're basically two levers joined at a pivot.
Things with handles.Drawer: Drawers pull out on runners, and the handle is often called a pull, one of the few ones in a room you hold daily.
Things with handles.Basketball: A basketball has no handle, so it is dribbled and gripped by its pebbled surface instead.
Things with handles.Dinner plate: Plates have no handle, which is a trap, although a few old-style plates have small side grips.
Things with handles.Coin: A coin has no handle, but it is stamped with ridged edges that help blind people feel its value.
Things with handles.Pillow: A pillow has no handle, and some are shaped like a rectangle to fit under your head and shoulders.
Things with handles.Book: A book has no handle, though some old Bibles and scrolls had rollers or clasps for carrying.
Things with handles.Banana: A banana has no handle, but the stem is a convenient grip that many people hold while peeling.
Things with handles.Drinking glass: A simple drinking glass has no handle, unlike a beer stein or mug, which has one so warm hands don't heat the drink.
Things with handles.Brick: A brick has no handle, and its dimensions are sized so a bricklayer can hold it in one hand.
Things with handles.Frisbee: A Frisbee has no handle, and its rim lip is the part that makes it stable in flight.
Things with handles.Pencil: A pencil has no handle, but the wooden barrel is hexagonal so it doesn't roll off a desk.
Things with handles.Sock: A sock has no handle, and it's among the most frequently lost items in laundry.
Things with handles.Egg: An egg has no handle, and its dome shape is surprisingly strong when pressure is applied end to end.

Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Snowmobile: Canadian inventor Joseph-Armand Bombardier popularized the snowmobile in the 1950s and 60s, and his company later grew into a giant of transport.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Sled: Archaeologists have found sleds thousands of years old, which means people were gliding over snow long before they used wheels on ice.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Toboggan: The word comes from an Algonquin term for a flat, runnerless sled, and the design suits deep powder because it floats rather than cuts in.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Bobsled: Bobsleds got their name from early crews who bobbed back and forth to gain speed, and modern four-man sleds can top 140 km/h.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Sleigh: Unlike a plain sled, a sleigh is built to carry passengers in comfort, often with bells so that others could hear it coming over muffled snow.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Snowcat: Snowcats are tracked machines that groom ski slopes overnight, and some are fitted with winches to haul themselves up the steepest pistes.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Snowplow: Because a plow's blade pushes snow aside rather than lifting it, cities also pre-spread salt, which lowers water's freezing point to keep roads clear.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Dog sled: Dog sled teams carried diphtheria serum to Nome, Alaska, in 1925, and the Iditarod race commemorates that relay across frozen wilderness.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Luge: Luge riders lie on their backs, feet first, steering with subtle leg and shoulder pressure, and they reach speeds near 140 km/h.
Vehicles designed for snow or ice.Icebreaker: Icebreakers don't just smash ice: their sloped bows ride up onto it so the ship's weight breaks it from above, and some nuclear-powered ones work in Russia.
